title: Silence, course of dealing, and unsolicited goods
shortTitle: Silence, course of dealing, and unsolicited goods
summary: Silence ordinarily does not accept an offer. Prior dealings, knowingly accepted services, or other circumstances can give silence a different significance.
notes:
An offeror cannot ordinarily impose a contract merely by announcing that failure to reject will count as agreement. Hobbs considers retained goods against a history of similar transactions; American Bronze considers a regular ordering practice. In goods cases involving additional terms, silence may have a statutory effect distinct from accepting an offer. In consumer cases such as Klocek, retaining the product did not establish express agreement to newly supplied terms on the record presented.

An offeror cannot ordinarily impose acceptance by declaring that failure to reject counts as assent. Hobbs concerns retention of skins after repeated comparable transactions, and American Bronze concerns a longstanding ordering-and-production practice. The book distinguishes these contexts from unsolicited merchandise and from subscriptions in which the recipient has already agreed to a negative-option arrangement. This is a source account, not a current compliance guide.
